  Agent Factory is a set of AI agents that build software from a backlog of stories. A story is one piece of work on its own branch. A developer agent writes a story's code. A code-review agent reads the change and files each problem as a finding. Then automatic checks, called gates, measure the code. One gate computes a CRAP score, short for Change Risk Anti-Patterns, which rates how risky a function is to change.

A story can run in two ways. In an orchestrated run, the implementation agent starts stories in parallel waves and merges each one itself. When a human drives by hand, the human starts one story at a time and merges it. Today the two paths follow different procedures. The orchestrated path blocks a merge that fails the gates, but reviews no story before the feature is done. So a defect reaches the merged code, and the next wave builds on it. The hand-driven path reviews each story, but its gates rest on an instruction to the agent, and an instruction leaves no trace. So a function with a CRAP score of 42 against a threshold of 30 can merge by hand, while an orchestrated run blocks it.

The proposal gives both paths one story workflow. The developer agent implements the story and commits. The code-review agent reviews the branch, and the agent fixes findings until none is open. Then the gates run, the agent fixes what they report and commits, and the branch goes to the merge. The paths differ only in how a story starts and who merges it.

Every story passes the merge, so the checks run there. A merge check script reads the head of the story branch. It refuses the branch when no review of the story exists, when a finding for the story is open, or when a gate fails. It reruns the gates and trusts no stored result. So the function with a score of 42 now fails on both paths. In an orchestrated run, the script refuses the merge. By hand, the agent runs the script before handing the branch back. The agent's report to the human includes the script's output, so the human sees the failure.

  A reader might expect the review at the end of a feature to be enough. It stays, because it shows how stories fit together. But one story's change is small enough to read in full, and a defect is cheapest to fix before another story builds on it.

The developer agent commits on both paths, so review and gates see committed work. Each finding names its story, so the script knows which findings belong to the branch. The test-strategy agent still owns the gates and their thresholds. The script checks only that a review ran and that its findings are closed, not whether the review was good.

  The proposal has no open questions. A separate proposal will decide which findings may stay unfixed. Until then, the agent fixes every open finding.
